# Basic Architecture Overview

## Executables
The **Proka Executable** ([`proka-exec`](https://github.com/RainSTR-Studio/proka-exec)) is an executable format developed by *RainSTR Studio*. 
Since the PE/ELF, and other executable formats cannot satisfy the requirements of ProkaOS, the PKE (*the short form of Proka Executable*) came out to solve these problems.

Furthermore, It's much more simple to parse than PE/ELF, which means it can save you a lot of time parsing PKE.

See also: *Part II: Proka Executable*

## Bootloaders
The **Proka Bootloader** ([`proka-bootloader`](https://github.com/RainSTR-Studio/proka-bootloader)) is a standalone bootloader, created on Mar. 7, 2026, written by *RainSTR Studio*.

About bootloaders, here's an interesting story:

- When this project was created, we planned to use GRUB's *multiboot2* protocol at first. But *multiboot2* only takes us to 32-bit mode, so we can only write a stub to switch to 64-bit mode. It's hard, so soon we deprecated this plan.
- Then we use *limine* instead. We accept that it's a great bootloader, but that's not enough - *zhangxuan2011*, a member of *RainSTR Studio*, wants to make up a self-developed bootloader, but it delayed for several months. 
- On Mar. 7, 2026, he started the main developing process. 1 month later, the `proka-bootloader` is basically usable. Now the current version of kernel is based on it.

For more information, see also: *Part III: Proka Bootloader*

## Kernel
The **Proka Kernel** ([`proka-kernel`](https://github.com/RainSTR-Studio/proka-kernel)) is the core part of ProkaOS. Without this component, the ProkaOS won't run.

The core design is mostly in kernel. We are now separating them to describe one by one.

### Process Model
Just as 1.2 mentions, the ProkaOS separated the process into 2 parts: **Driver Process** and **Normal Process**. For convenience, we'd like to call them as **DPD** (*Driver Process Domain*) and **NPD** (*Normal Process Domain*).

See also: *Part IV: Process Model*

### SMS/DMS
**SMS/DMS**, is the short form of *Syscall Management System/Driver Call Management System*, or *SDMS* shorter, is a part of kernel, which connects each drivers and normal process.

Drivers can register syscall or drvcall (*Driver Call*) in their runtime, and they can choose one favorite syscall/drvcall number (0..GRLEN - 1), even more than one syscall/drvcall.

The user program or driver can use a way (will explain in ahead) to get syscall/drvcall table, and invoke them directly.

*NOTE*: Only driver can register syscall/drvcall; for normal programs, it's unnessary and unsafe.

See also: *Part V: SMS/DMS*
